scenario: The retrieval track has 10 papers today, 5 with deep dives, centered on reranking and agentic search. ACARe finds that simply giving the reranker the original question clearly lifts a search agent's answer accuracy, with dedicated training adding a little more. A systems evaluation warns that before replacing a dedicated reranker with a large model, teams should tune the existing reranker's truncation policy. DecisionRAG drops the retriever and lets a decision model browse documents level by level. SkillQR mines rewriting skills from the corpus, and CA-HNM filters hard negatives with a knowledge graph. Teams working on search reranking or RAG can start with ACARe and the reranker-replacement study.

papers.title: CA-HNM: Constraint-Aware Hard Negative Mining for Dense Retrieval with Structured Domain Models
papers.authors: Ngoc Luyen Le, Marie-Hélène Abel, Bertrand Laforge
papers.abstract: Dense retrievers are commonly trained with hard negatives selected from lexical or dense retrieval results. Retrieval proximity, however, does not indicate whether a candidate conflicts with explicit domain structure. We introduce CA-HNM, a constraint-aware hard-negative mining framework that combines retrieval-based candidate generation with deterministic incompatibility rules derived from a structured domain model. The framework removes known positives, constructs a local typed context around the query target, records relational, scope, target, and level mismatches, and uses the resulting candidates to fine-tune a standard dual encoder. Structured information is required only during offline negative construction. We evaluate CA-HNM on MOOCCubeX and Course-Skill Atlas with two encoders, two training losses, and ten seeds. Relative to a retrieval-rank-matched control, CA-HNM-Pure has higher mean NDCG@10 in six of eight dataset--encoder--loss configurations. Four hierarchical 95% bootstrap intervals are entirely above zero, mostly under triplet loss. In a separate experiment, CA-HNM-Mixed shows slightly higher mean NDCG@10 than a matched-mixed control on both collections. Structural variants show that changes in available structure can also change candidate eligibility and negative-pool composition. The results indicate that the contribution of constraint-aware selection depends on the training objective and the composition of the negative pool.
papers.summary: Dense retrievers usually take hard negatives from top-ranked documents that are not labeled positive, but ranking high only shows a document resembles the query, not why it should be excluded. CA-HNM checks each candidate against a course knowledge graph, wrong concept, wrong scope or wrong difficulty level, and keeps only those with a clear conflict as negatives. It beats a rank-matched control without the graph in most settings, yet randomly shuffling the graph on one dataset raises NDCG@10 from 0.0311 to 0.1174, so how much the graph helps is still open.

deep_reading.title: CA-HNM: Constraint-Aware Hard Negative Mining for Dense Retrieval with Structured Domain Models

papers.title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models
papers.authors: Chao Wan, Paul Jünger, Beixi Du, Bodong Liu, Navaneetha Krishnan, Kilian Q. Weinberger
papers.abstract: While language models have become dramatically more capable, retrieval still largely relies on lexical matching or similarity in fixed embedding spaces. This creates a capability asymmetry: what the retriever fails to find, even the strongest generator cannot recover. We propose DecisionRAG, which brings the capabilities of pretrained language models to retrieval using decision models that jointly evaluate candidate branches in a single forward pass, without generating any tokens, and show that judging candidates in a shared context makes their relevance estimates comparable. Like a person browsing a library, DecisionRAG navigates the corpus's inherent structure from broad topics down to individual passages, deciding at each level which branches are worth exploring. Without task-specific training or a first-stage retriever, DecisionRAG outperforms dense retrieval with an 8B reranker by 13.8 R@1 points on MultiDoc2Dial and 17.4 Hit@1 points on Natural Questions. Across four benchmarks, including a corpus of 2.68 million Wikipedia paragraphs, retrieval takes just 0.7-1.8 seconds per query.
papers.summary: Most RAG systems still retrieve with BM25 or vector similarity, and evidence the retriever misses cannot be recovered by any generator. DecisionRAG drops the retriever and has a decision model browse like a person in a library, from topics to pages to passages, judging each level's candidates together in one context. Over 2.68 million Wikipedia passages its Hit@1 is 17.4 points above Qwen3-Embedding-8B retrieval plus a reranker, at about 1.7 seconds per query.

deep_reading.title: Retriever-Free Retrieval: Navigating Documents with Decision Models

papers.title: ACARE: Agent-Context-Aware Reranker for Iterative Search
papers.authors: Sahel Sharifymoghaddam, Yauhen Babakhin, Reza Esfandiarpoor, Oliver Holworthy, Jimmy Lin, Bo Liu
papers.abstract: In agentic search, a document can match an agent-generated sub-query without helping answer the user's original question. Conventional rerankers score documents against the sub-query alone, overlooking the broader task and the agent's reasoning. We introduce the Agent-Context-Aware Reranker (ACARe), a compact 4B LLM trained to rerank documents using this context when available. Across multiple benchmarks and agent families, ACARe improves retrieval quality over its base reranker while reducing search effort. These benefits extend to answer generation: ACARe improves accuracy and reduces searches over no reranking, while matching or exceeding the base reranker's mean accuracy with more precise evidence. It also helps smaller agents narrow the retrieval-quality gap to larger agents, showing how better retrieval tools can make smaller agents more effective. The model, training data, and code will be released soon.
papers.summary: Search agents often send sub-queries of just a few keywords, so a sub-query-only reranker promotes documents that match the words but do not help the real question. ACARe gives the reranker the original question and the agent's reasoning too. The key control: without changing Qwen3-Reranker-4B's weights, adding the question alone lifts a small agent's accuracy from 48.2% to 54.8%, and fine-tuning brings it to 57.6%. Most of the gain comes from the context itself, and all five agents need fewer searches.

deep_reading.title: ACARE: Agent-Context-Aware Reranker for Iterative Search

papers.title: SkillQR: Agentic Skill Discovery for Reason-Intensive Query Rewriting
papers.authors: Kenan Jiang, Meixiu Long, Zihao Zhang, Ran Xu, Eugene Agichtein, Fei Liu
papers.abstract: Dense retrievers provide grounded evidence that mitigates hallucinations in outputs from Large Language Models (LLMs). Real-world queries are often verbose, ambiguously framed, or require multi-step reasoning, introducing irrelevant details that weaken semantic matching for dense retrievers. Query rewriting is a widely adopted pre-retrieval technique that leverages LLMs to reformulate queries and bridge the semantic gap between such queries and the retrieval target. Existing rewriting approaches either rely on expensive proprietary models, substantial training data, or iterative retrieval and rewriting, while largely applying a uniform rewriting strategy regardless of the retrieval corpus. We observe that effective query rewriting instructions are not universal: the optimal strategy depends on the retrieval target, rather than the model alone. We introduce SkillQR, a query rewriting framework that automatically discovers reasoning strategy sets from the retrieval target and dynamically routes a query to the appropriate rewriting strategy at inference time. Without relying on training data, SkillQR achieves competitive performance compared to fine-tuned rewriting models on the BRIGHT and R2MED benchmarks, while also providing lower inference latency than iterative rewriting approaches.
papers.summary: LLM query rewriting usually applies one instruction to every query, yet the right direction for a rewrite depends on the corpus. SkillQR clusters the corpus offline and has an LLM write a few rewrite instructions for the document types, such as listing the required data structures and algorithms; at query time the same model picks one before rewriting, with no training data. Its mined skills match hand-written subject prompts, and the 14B version takes about 38 seconds per query versus 85 for iterative ThinkQE, showing what dropping multi-round iteration saves.

deep_reading.title: SkillQR: Agentic Skill Discovery for Reason-Intensive Query Rewriting

papers.title: Can System-1-Style Decision Models Replace Dedicated Rerankers in RAG? A Systems Evaluation
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems often use a dedicated reranker to choose which retrieved candidates reach the language model. Reranking improves relevance but adds latency, so teams look for faster alternatives. System-1style decision models make direct, structured predictions instead of generating long responses. Could one provide comparable reranking quality with less inference overhead? We first screen 21 open-weight models on 11 benchmarks, then compare a promising decision model with a dedicated reranker on identical candidate lists. The default decision-model setup fails on many long candidate sets, so scoring only the requests it completes gives a misleading ranking. Limiting candidate text length largely restores reliability and makes some configurations competitive. A frozen evaluation on new retrieval data supports the reliability and ranking results, but confirms the latency requirement for only one of the two selected configurations. Across workloads, which model ranks better changes, and a tuned reranker remains faster and uses far less GPU memory. A decision model can perform competitive reranking, but replacing a reranker requires weighing quality, latency and memory together, and teams should tune the reranker they already run first.
papers.summary: If a team wants to replace its RAG reranker with a large model, this paper says to tune the existing reranker first. Comparing the 27B decision model PPLX Decider with the 0.6B Jina v3.5 on identical candidates, default PPLX returns valid results for only 44.1% of requests; it looks better on completed requests but clearly loses once failures count. Splitting the input budget evenly and keeping each candidate's opening lets it match Jina, yet Jina with the same truncation drops to 245 ms and needs a fraction of the memory.

deep_reading.title: Can System-1-Style Decision Models Replace Dedicated Rerankers in RAG? A Systems Evaluation

papers.title: Ranking Is Not Deciding: Benchmark Shortcuts and Operating-Point Collapse in Query-Time RAG Poisoning Defenses
papers.abstract: Query-time filters that screen each retrieved document before it reaches the generator are the dominant published defense against retrieval-augmented generation poisoning, and they report near-perfect detection on domain benchmarks. We show that this performance is predicted by how the poison set was built rather than by what the filter reads: removing a single construction cue destroys the deployed decision before it destroys the ranking. Two label-free statistics of a poison set and its clean corpus profile the cue: containment, how often the target question appears verbatim in the poison, and length overlap. PoisonedRAG's released code prepends the target question to every inserted passage. Of the 21 published defense evaluations we survey, 8 verifiably run poison built this way and 5 substitute a length cue; separately, 12 report no false-positive rate at the operating point they deploy. Deleting only that prefix from the attack authors' own passages (0.93 still retrieved for their target) takes RAGuard, a published content filter we re-implement, from AUROC 0.953 to 0.758 and its miss rate from 0.191 to 0.763. Across four corpora, four attack families and ten per-document defenses on one shared candidate set, the profile predicts where detection saturates. Padding medical poison to clean length with word-shuffled filler that carries no content takes TrustRAG's set-level stage from a miss rate of 0.000 to 0.827, and one learned scorer of ours from 0.000 to 0.986 (0.321 at a matched 5% false-positive rate) while its AUROC holds at 0.953. The ranking survives; the decision does not. A defense-aware attacker defeats our own scorer, so we claim no defense. A detection result is evidence only when it is reported with its poison set's construction profile and the false-positive rate at the threshold actually deployed; we release the script that computes the profile.
papers.summary: RAG poisoning defenses often report near-perfect detection, but this paper finds much of it comes from how poison sets are built: PoisonedRAG's code prepends the target question to every poison passage. Deleting only that prefix raises the published RAGuard filter's miss rate from 0.191 to 0.763, which means it mostly recognizes the prefix. The authors argue detection numbers mean little unless reported with the poison set's construction profile and the false-positive rate at the deployed threshold.

papers.title: Knowing When the Evidence Is Enough: Requirement-Directed Search with Horn-Closure Certificates
papers.abstract: After each Web search, a search-augmented model must decide whether its evidence suffices: answer, search again, or abstain. Prevailing systems leave this to holistic model judgement, which can accept a context naming every entity yet lacking one required fact. We instead make sufficiency structural: a per-query requirement hypergraph states which facts jointly yield another fact. This raises two challenges: deriving requirements from the question alone, and linking each requirement to passages about the right entity. Certify therefore decomposes the question, searches per requirement, and accepts links only after entity checks. Horn closure over the links yields a certificate, the minimal sufficient passages and their derivation, or an abstention naming open requirements. Given correct retrieval, requirements and links, the decision is sound, and complete up to the entity check. Pooled over three corpora with unanswerable twins, Certify decides significantly more accurately than search agents, graph retrieval and sufficiency judges in default configurations. On the same evidence, it matches a proprietary model's sufficiency label without an additional model call. Over 21M Wikipedia passages, entity checks add 4 to 13 points of decision accuracy where gold evidence exists. Finally, answers from its certificate are 80% correct, against 57% from all retrieved passages.
papers.summary: After each search, a search-augmented model must decide whether its evidence suffices: answer, search again, or abstain. Leaving this to holistic model judgement lets it answer when every entity is mentioned but one required fact is missing. Certify splits the question into fact requirements, stating which facts together yield the next, and searches for each; a passage satisfies a requirement only if it is about the right entity. It answers only when the requirements derive the answer, and otherwise names what is missing. Over 21 million Wikipedia passages, answers from its minimal evidence set are 80% correct versus 57% from all retrieved passages.

papers.title: CalibraRL: Confidence-Calibrated Reinforcement Learning for Mitigating Hallucinations in RAG
papers.authors: Qianchi Zhang, Hainan Zhang, Liang Pang, Hongwei Zheng, Zhiming Zheng
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce plausible but incorrect answers, motivating reinforcement learning methods that reward correct answers, penalize incorrect answers, and allow abstention. However, fixed outcome-based rewards do not distinguish incorrect responses with different confidence levels or account for differences in answering reliability across queries. Consequently, such rewards may inadequately penalize overconfident errors and fail to discourage unnecessary abstention. We propose CalibraRL, a reinforcement learning framework that incorporates response confidence and query-level answering evidence into reward design. For non-abstaining responses, CalibraRL combines correctness-based utility with a Brier-based penalty that encourages agreement between confidence and correctness. For abstentions, it estimates conditional answering reliability using a Beta posterior derived from the correctness of non-abstaining responses within each sampled group. The abstention reward increases with the posterior probability that the model's accuracy on non-abstaining responses is below a predefined threshold. CalibraRL reuses training rollouts without requiring additional annotations indicating whether the model knows the answer to each question. Experiments on three QA datasets demonstrate that CalibraRL improves answer precision and reduces hallucinations compared with strong baselines. Further analysis shows that CalibraRL reduces mean expected calibration error (ECE) by 30.8\% across two backbone models and three datasets, highlighting its potential to improve the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in web search.
papers.summary: When RL teaches a model to abstain when unsure, typical rewards penalize every wrong answer equally and give abstention a fixed reward, ignoring confidence. CalibraRL adds a Brier penalty based on confidence and correctness, so confident errors cost more. For abstention, it estimates from other rollouts of the same question whether the model can answer reliably, rewarding abstention more when it cannot. It needs no extra labels, reduces hallucination on three QA datasets, and cuts mean calibration error by 30.8%.

papers.title: Evolve on Graph: Self-Evolving Knowledge Graph Reasoning without Question Annotations
papers.authors: Zongyuan Sun, Shuai Zhao, Ke Shu, Ziyue Zhu, Shangyang Wu, Yuanlin Lin, Tao Wang, Shiyue Li, Yingjun Du, Anh Tuan Luu, Haoran Luo
papers.abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) provide reliable external knowledge for multi-hop factual reasoning with large language models (LLMs), yet most KGs in real-world domains such as finance and industry lack question--answer (QA) annotations. Without such annotations, existing methods struggle to improve LLM graph reasoning: training-free agents cannot improve their exploration through interaction; reinforcement learning (RL) agents depend on QA data annotated by humans or synthesized by closed-source models; and training data is typically built offline, so its topology mix is fixed and cannot follow the agent's ability. We propose Evolve on Graph (EoG), a framework that lets an LLM self-evolve its graph reasoning without any QA annotations. Through Graph Self-Play, a single LLM alternates between a Proposer that poses questions and a Solver that answers them. To make questions verifiable, Symbolically Verifiable Topology Synthesis (SVTS) samples reasoning topologies on the KG and executes the corresponding first-order logic queries, yielding topology skeletons with correct and complete answer sets; guided by a skeleton, the Proposer explores the graph to pose a multi-hop question. To let task topologies follow the Solver, a Boundary-Aware Graph Curriculum rewards the Proposer by the Solver's score variance, keeping questions at the Solver's capability boundary so that complex topologies enter training as the Solver improves. On six benchmarks over Freebase, Wikidata, and an industrial KG, EoG consistently outperforms prompting-, retrieval-, and agent-based methods, showing that LLM graph reasoning can improve through self-play without QA annotations. Our code is available at https://github.com/Szy5/EoG
papers.summary: Knowledge graphs in finance or industry rarely have QA annotations, so there is no data to improve LLM multi-hop graph reasoning with RL. EoG has one model alternate between proposer and solver: it samples reasoning structures on the graph and executes logic queries for exact answers, and the proposer writes multi-hop questions from them. The solver answers each question several times, and the proposer is rewarded most when results are mixed, not for questions that are too easy or too hard, keeping questions at the edge of the solver's ability. On six benchmarks over Freebase, Wikidata and an industrial graph, it beats prompting, retrieval and agent methods.

papers.title: FormBench: A Benchmark for Fine-Grained Retrieval in Formulation Patents
papers.authors: Vineeth Venugopal, Elsa Olivetti, Jonathan Welch
papers.abstract: We introduce FormBench, a platform for testing the ability of models to retrieve precise chemical information from technical documents. FormBench contains 55,352 queries and two retrieval corpus variants each with ~1M passages: FormBench-Random (C0), with randomly sampled distractors, and FormBench-Structured (C1), with structurally proximate distractors. Each query is paired with an anchor passage, a hard negative, and a soft negative - derived from a materials ontology through entity overlap scoring, providing a deeper graded signal on a model's discriminatory power. We evaluate 10 model configurations spanning commercial API encoders (OpenAI, Voyage), open-source encoders (Nomic, GTE-large, Qwen3-Embed), and their task-adaptive fine-tuned (TAPT) variants. We find: (1) commercial APIs score very poorly across all configurations (OpenAI-3-large: 0.009 on C1, 0.213 on C0); (2) TAPT on FormBench triplets lifts Qwen3-Embed to 0.4085 on C1, 0.4835 on C0; (3) BM25 remains competitive (0.375 on C1, 0.467 on C0), exceeded only by TAPT-Qwen3; (4) corpus size has a significant impact on retrieval behavior, as demonstrated through a corpus-size ablation; (5) the API failure traces to within-domain geometric collapse; (6) APIs outperform even the TAPT variants on classification and clustering tasks. FormBench is released in BEIR-compatible format at huggingface.co/datasets/vinven7/FormBench under CC-BY-4.0.
papers.summary: In formulation patents, relevant and distracting passages often name the same chemicals and differ only in the role they play, which generic embedding models struggle with. FormBench tests this with over 55,000 queries, with distractors chosen through a materials taxonomy to share most chemicals with the answer but differ in function. The results are striking: OpenAI's commercial embedding scores just 0.009 nDCG@10 on the hard corpus against 0.375 for BM25, which means the generic space collapses within the domain; only Qwen3-Embed fine-tuned on the benchmark's triplets beats BM25.
